entries.title: As Cubs aim to upgrade pitching at trade deadline, high-scoring hitters show what’s possible in playoffs
entries.summary: <p>ST. LOUIS – When Jed Hoyer’s front office wraps its work at the trade deadline Monday, don’t expect to see any big additions to the lineup.</p><p>Obviously, the team’s focus <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/17/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-rumors-starting-pitching-jed-hoyer-front-office" >will be on improving a pitching staff</a> that’s already had its depth stretched to its limits amid an avalanche of summer injuries.</p><p>But adding arms doesn’t just demand a higher priority. The team’s position players have been good enough that significant midseason augmentation in that area is simply not necessary.</p><p>“Our position-playing group is really, really good,” Hoyer said at the start of the second half. “That’s a group that could win a lot of games in October.”</p><p>The Cubs’ bats have made Hoyer’s prediction look like a good one of late, posting big run totals and establishing themselves as one of the sport’s best lineups – one that indeed could fuel a deep playoff run.</p><p>Even in a season that saw a lineup-wide power outage for a month, the Cubs came into Wednesday as baseball’s No. 3 team in runs scored, with 558 of them, trailing only the Nationals and Pirates, two teams they’re ahead of in the crowded NL wild-card race.</p><p>They scored 35 of those runs in their previous four games, with run totals of 11, 7, 7 and 10. They scored double-digit runs four times in their first 11 games following the All-Star break.</p><p>And since the end of that early-summer slump, there’s arguably been no better offensive team than the Cubs, who woke up Wednesday leading the sport in runs scored (250), on-base percentage (.355) and walks (169), second in slugging percentage (.465) and OPS (.820) and third in batting average (.269), doubles (79) and triples (10) since June 11.</p><p>It’s not just a helpful turnaround – one the Cubs were plenty confident was coming during their doldrums – but a consistent offensive output that could make them as fearsome a postseason foe as any team.</p><p>“We have so many good players in this lineup that play every day,” left fielder Ian Happ said Tuesday, “and I have all the confidence in the world this group is going to put up those kinds of numbers, because that’s who we are.</p><p>“You saw it early in the year, we were a top-five offense, and then we had those [few] weeks of not producing. Then you get hot like this. It ebbs and flows. There’s a lot of belief in the players in the room.”</p><p>How dangerous could these Cubs be to opposing pitchers, even the caliber of arms they’ll see in the playoffs?</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/25/cubs-pete-crow-armstrong-mvp-paul-skenes-pirates-cy-young-ian-happ-matthew-boyd-shota-imanaga" >Just ask Pirates ace Paul Skenes</a>, the reigning NL Cy Young winner who gave up five runs to the Cubs last weekend.</p><p>Or ask their teammates. Inside the Cubs’ clubhouse, pitchers are certain about one thing: They’re happy they don’t have to figure out a way to get through this lineup.</p><p>“I think about that all the time, honestly,” righty Colin Rea said with a smile. “You’ve got Pete [Crow-Armstrong] at the top of the lineup to start the game, that’s not someone you want to face off the bat.</p><p>“It’s a good, balanced lineup that can get on base but also do damage.”</p><p>And of course, this is the same group of players responsible for the team’s status as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/24/game-saving-defense-fires-up-cubs-in-thick-of-division-race-were-at-that-point-every-game-matters" >the best defensive squad in baseball</a>.</p><p>Throw it all together, and yes, Mr. Hoyer, this indeed looks like a group capable of powering a great many October victories.</p><p>Of course, there is a reason Hoyer & Co. are on the prowl for pitching, and that’s an area that needs to be fortified <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/25/cubs-playoffs-brewers-pirates-nl-central-matthew-boyd-starting-rotation" >if the Cubs are to avoid the same fate they suffered last fall</a>, when pitching-depth issues helped them to an earlier-than-desired playoff exit against the division-rival Brewers.</p><p>But with these position players as a foundation, belief in a different outcome is far from unwarranted.</p><p>“The one thing that’s been so consistent is, obviously, the position-player group that has, fortunately, been able to stay healthy and show up every day and play and continue to stack winning baseball on top of each other,” shortstop Dansby Swanson said earlier this month. “There’s so much room for this team to continue to grow and get better and play better.”</p>

entries.summary: <p>A man was shot in North Lawndale Wednesday afternoon, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The 56-year-old man was near the sidewalk in the 1200 block of South Harding Avenue at 5:50 p.m. when he was shot in the thigh, police said. entries.title: Latino high schools hit especially hard by teacher cuts in CPS budget heading for vote
entries.summary: <p>Veteran teacher Anna Acosta shudders to think how Kelly High School students will react when they show up next month and find that a beloved dean is gone.</p><p>She suspects the dean’s layoff will especially hit the school’s recent immigrants who looked to her for support.</p><p>“She was extremely, extremely helpful in building bridges and also repairing harm, and she was well-respected,” said Acosta, who teaches history at the high school in Brighton Park on the Southwest Side. “I am sure my students are going to say, ‘Where's Miss Montoya? We loved her.’”</p><p>And it’s not just one dean. Kelly also lost five teacher positions, plus two interventionists who helped struggling students. The result: Fewer classes will be offered and the remaining ones will have more students.</p><p>High schools like Kelly are being hit hard by budget cuts that district officials acknowledge will affect the student experience. When laying out the budget earlier this month, the district said it was cutting nearly 1,000 core instructional positions, which include English and math teachers, as well as art teachers.</p><p>But Chicago Public Schools only publicly released information on how exactly budget cuts are impacting individual schools on Monday — just days before Thursday’s budget vote and weeks later than it typically shares this information.</p><p>A WBEZ analysis of school-level budget changes shows that high schools with mostly Latino students are losing the most regular classroom teachers, both as a share of teachers and in overall positions. They lost 158 teachers, or 7% of their teachers.</p><p>Overall, there are about 4% fewer teachers across all schools, not including teachers who work specifically with students in special education. WBEZ analyzed teacher losses by type of school and student demographics.</p><p>Supt. Macquline King called the budget challenging and, as a former principal, she said it was hard for her to know that these cuts touch students. But she noted that principals, with their local school councils, make a lot of the decisions about who to lay off and who to keep.</p><p>“Those schools and those communities know what their children need most, and we're relying on them to inform those budgets,” she said.</p><p>There’s two coinciding reasons Latino high schools experienced the deepest cuts. To close a massive budget deficit, the school district increased the number of students each teacher can take on. At the same time, many predominantly Latino high schools have seen their enrollments decrease.</p><p>Kelly’s enrollment dipped by about 100 students last school year.</p><p>Norma Rios-Sierra, a school board member who represents the Northwest Side, said she has heard from principals in her part of the city who are trying to figure out how to make their budgets work with the cuts. Her district’s only neighborhood high school, Roosevelt, is down eight teacher positions, according to CPS data.</p><p>She said those losses stem from enrollment decreases and an effort by the district to make sure that schools are equitably funded. When the district has limited resources it ends up pitting schools against each other, she said.</p><p>She worries that each staff loss is detrimental, and the stress put on schools “translates to the students’ experience.”</p><p>The school-level information also reveals that other programs and staff that weren’t discussed during initial budget presentations are being cut. There’s half as much money to pay for staff or organizations to put school safety plans in place.</p><p>Forty schools lost school assistants who, like at Kelly, often serve in the role of a dean, while two dozen schools lost their tech coordinator.</p><p>One Northwest side principal said her high school of more than 1,000 students now has just a part-time position for a tech coordinator. She said she had to eliminate her full-time tech coordinator along with six other positions. She did not want to be identified because CPS did not give her permission to be interviewed.</p><p>She and her staff had big plans for next school year, she said, but the cuts “took the wind out of their sails.”</p><p>Many schools are getting less discretionary funding that principals often use to pay for after-school programs or other staff like lunchroom monitors.</p><p>And more schools are having to use discretionary funds to pay for teachers or assistant principals, which also takes money away from other programs.</p><p>Kia Banks, the president of the Chicago Principals and Administrators Association, said it is not right to make principals use their limited pots of discretionary funding to pay for positions that the district should provide. She was blindsided in the spring when the district announced it would no longer cover assistant principal positions at schools with smaller enrollments.</p><p>Banks points out that most of the displaced assistant principals are Black women who work in South and West side schools. She said the union is still negotiating with the district to try to win those positions back. She does not think the school board should pass the budget as is on Thursday because it lacks “the staffing and services our students need.”</p><p>WBEZ did not analyze school-level changes in special education teachers or aides. CPS budgeted for more special education staff this year than it did last year. However, the district adds special education staff as the school year goes on and there are now more students identified as having disabilities, as well as students with rising needs.</p><p>This summer, CPS laid off or eliminated vacancies for about 1,800 special education staff, but many of those positions will be added back as the school year goes on.</p>

entries.title: 2 teens shot in Greater Grand Crossing
entries.summary: <p>Two teens were shot in Greater Grand Crossing Wednesday afternoon, according to Chicago police.</p><p>An 18-year-old and 13-year-old were inside an apartment building in the 400 block of Winneconna Parkway at 4:05 p.m. when someone in the hallway fired into the apartment, police said.</p><p>The elder boy was shot in the neck, clavicle and back and was taken to University of Chicago Medical Center in critical condition. The 13-year-old boy was grazed on both calves and taken to Comer Children’s Hospital in good condition.</p><p>No one is in custody.</p>

entries.title: Improbable rallies carry White Sox past Yankees in 12 innings
entries.summary: <p>After six innings Wednesday, no one could’ve thought the Yankees and White Sox would play six more.</p><p>But they did, and Sox catcher Edgar Quero ended the bonkers game with a single in the 12th for an improbable 6-5 victory, the team’s eighth walk-off win this season.</p><p>“The opportunity to get one here, the way that they did it, just to continue to battle,” Sox manager Will Venable said. “We’ve seen it, we’ve talked about it before. [It] was awesome.”</p><p>The Yankees jumped on Sox starter Davis Martin for four runs in the first, but he kept them in check for the next five innings. Meanwhile, the Sox couldn’t touch fireballer Cam Schlittler, who retired the first 11 batters before Miguel Vargas singled. Then he retired the next seven.</p><p>The game began to turn in the seventh when Schlittler was pulled after a run-scoring double by Andrew Benintendi. In the eighth, Yankees manager Aaron Boone turned to righty Paul Blackburn with a runner on second. Sam Antonacci greeted him with a two-run homer, and Munetaka Murakami followed with a solo shot to tie it.</p><p>After the Yankees took the lead in the 11th, they gifted the Sox a run in the bottom half. With automatic runner Murakami on third, catcher Ali Sanchez needlessly tried to pick him off and ended up throwing the ball down the left-field line.</p><p>“I was surprised they [tried to] pick me off,” Murakami said. “I was a little bit off the bag, obviously, but I was hearing [third-base coach Justin Jirschele] clearly, so I was able to get back in time.”</p><p>The Yankees loaded the bases in the 12th against Jordan Hicks but came away empty. Hicks struck out Ben Rice swinging and induced Sanchez to ground out — but not without drama.</p><p>“Not the way I drew it up, but it worked out,” Hicks said. “I felt like today was the hardest I’ve thrown all season; 0-2 to 3-2, though, on the last batter, bases loaded, had to throw a few strikes there.”</p><p>In the bottom half, Chase Meidroth sacrificed automatic runner Tristan Peters to third, and Quero, who entered the game in the eighth with a .181 batting average, brought him home.</p><p>“Good feelings, especially right now,” he said. “[It’s been a] tough year for me.”</p><h3>‘We need more wand’</h3><p>The White Sox released a video on social media in which an unsuspecting Mike Vasil was summoned to Venable’s office, where general manager Chris explained that Vasil’s wand had caught the attention of the commissioner’s office and that the team needed to “change something up.” He asked for suggestions from Vasil, who looked concerned.</p><p>Then Getz called in third-base coach Justin Jirschele, who explained the “problem” to Vasil.</p><p>“We need more wand,” said Jirschele, who handed Vasil a Harry Potter wand. “How does 20,000 sound for our fans? Congratulations on your first promotion.”</p><p>“You realize you really got me?” Vasil said. “I was like, what do I do now? I don’t have an identity.”</p><p>On Sept. 4, the first 20,000 fans attending the game against the Twins will receive wands. Asked what Rate Field will look like that night, Venable said, “I don’t know, but that’s a lot of magic.”</p><h3>Notes</h3><p>Venable was asked about Noah Schultz’s status after the rookie lefty lasted only 3 ⅓ innings Monday against the Yankees. He’s on track to pitch Friday against the Rays.</p><p>“We’ll announce the next series rotation here in the next day or two,” Venable said. “The plan is for Noah to be on this team and in the rotation as we’re evaluating the next cycle.”</p><p>• NBC Sports flexed the Sox’ game Sept. 6 against the Twins to “Sunday Night Baseball.” The game will air on NBC Sports Network and Peacock. First pitch is scheduled for 5:20 p.m.</p><p>It will be the Sox’ first “SNB” game at Rate Field since Aug. 9, 2020 (vs. Guardians), and their first with fans in the ballpark since July 29, 2008 (vs. entries.title: Dear Abby: Needy neighbor is constantly asking for things
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I moved into my apartment four months ago. While my sister, her son and I were moving things in, my new next-door neighbor introduced herself. She has since become intrusive. I am an introvert, and she knocks on my door wanting everything from plastic bags to cigarettes and alcohol. Every day since I moved here, she has been asking for something. She came six times yesterday. I'd like to be her friend, but she takes and I give. I'm tired. Help, please. — <i>OVERWHELMED IN OHIO</i></p><p><b>DEAR OVERWHELMED:</b> A way to fix this would be to tell your neighbor the truth. Tell her you would like to be a considerate neighbor, but you are not a convenience store and do not wish to be disturbed on a daily basis. Then, when she comes around asking for cigarettes, liquor or plastic bags (which are choking our landfills and our waterways), tell her you are fresh out — and repeat it as necessary. If she persists, discuss it with the management of your apartment building.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My brother-in-law is currently in a relationship with a woman who was intimate with my husband many years before we married. It was a one-night thing, but now she is with my BIL and is going to be at family functions. I'm afraid it's going to be awkward, and I'm not comfortable. My husband is supportive of whatever I choose to do. The rest of the family has no issue with it because, of course, it's not their issue. I need advice. — <i>IN A DILEMMA IN PENNSYLVANIA</i></p><p><b>DEAR DILEMMA:</b> This is not a dilemma unless you choose to make it one. A one-night stand is not a relationship, and the woman is not a cause for concern. What happened between them once, many years ago before your marriage, shouldn't be a threat to you or your relationship with your husband's family. If anyone is tasteless enough to bring it up, treat it with humor or say you don't wish to discuss it. Then act like the lady you are and be cordial.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I'm a 17-year-old guy, and I still suck my thumb, though I do it mostly when I'm in bed. I am going to college next year and I'm worried I might get outed by a roommate if I'm caught. Is my habit that unusual, and do you have any advice on how to stop it? It's like an addiction. — <i>EMBARRASSED IN THE WEST</i></p><p><b>DEAR EMBARRASSED:</b> You are not alone in having this problem. In the past, I have heard from other adults who suck their thumbs. Comfort yourself with the thought that it's not an addiction and not all that unusual. Stress has been known to cause people to suck their thumbs. One way to discourage the habit would be to keep yourself from becoming overly tired. Another would be to coat your thumbs with a bad-tasting substance. (Search online or ask your pharmacist to recommend something.) That, coupled with the fear of being ridiculed, may do the trick.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p><p>What teens need to know about sex, drugs, AIDS and getting along with peers and parents is in "What Every Teen Should Know." Send your name and mailing address, plus check or money order for $8 (U.S. funds) to: Dear Abby, Teen Booklet, P.O. Box 446, Kings Mills, OH 45034-0446. (Shipping and handling are included in the price.)</p>

entries.title: Imani Village brings senior housing with style to Cottage Grove Avenue
entries.summary: <p>For years, a stretch of Cottage Grove Avenue immediately south of 95th Street hasn't been much to write home about — just a run of small industrial buildings and vacant land on the east edge of the Metra Electric embankment.</p><p>The street's big draw? Maybe the Social Security Administration field office near 97th Street. And certainly in the olden days, the wonderful smell that used to come from Jays Potato Chips factory at 99th. The facility closed in 2007 and man, I still miss that aroma.</p><p>But the block now has a good looking new player that's worthy of attention: the $32 million Imani Village Senior Residences at 9621 S. Cottage Grove Ave.</p><p>Built by Trinity United Church of Christ — the progressive and socially active church is also a developer on the South Side — and designed by the Black-owned architectural firm Johnson & Lee, the broad five-story building wakes up the street with a dash of color and a bit of verve inspired by the Motherland.</p><p>Most importantly, the residences provide open space, well-designed lounge areas and affordable apartments in a corner of the city that needs and deserves it.</p><p>And more things are planned. Imani Village, Trinity's development entity, aims to redevelop 34 acres surrounding the senior residences.</p><p>"One of our main things in development is building a community that serves from sunrise to sunset [of life]," Imani Village Executive Vice President Patricia Eggleston said. "And of course, the latter years of your life, you need to be comfortable. You need to be in a nice surroundings. And so that's why we decided that we wanted to build it."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" "That's how we came up with the pattern around the windows."</p><p>Trinity's Afrocentric ministry also informed the design, Eggleston said.</p><p>"The outside of the building ... shows the statement that we want to make as a people who are proud of our culture," she said.</p><p>The result is a very pleasant building inside and out. In addition to the apartments, the property offer things like a salon, library, multipurpose room and wellness center.</p><p>An attached private open-air ground floor courtyard where residents can sit and gather is an especially nice touch.</p><p>A glass-walled hallway runs by the space, allowing residents to experience natural light and greenery without even entering the courtyard.</p><p>The apartment building's wide mass acts as a visual and sonic barrier protecting the courtyard from the traffic noise along Cottage Grove Avenue and the rattle-rattle of commuter and freight trains running along the embankment across the street.</p><p>"You got the train and etc.," Johnson said. The building's hallways, apartment entrances and common spaces are exceptionally well done, especially given the relatively low budget, thanks to the work of Black interior designer Brooke Lang.</p><p>A lounge area with a stone fireplace, snazzy brown patterned wallpaper and comfortable club chairs could pass for a section of a cool coffee shop.</p><p>"We really wanted to bring a sophistication to the space," Lange, owner of Brooke Lang Design said. entries.title: Other cities also struggle with teen takeovers. What can Chicago learn from them?
entries.summary: <p>Like Chicago and many other American cities, Baltimore has been grappling with teen takeovers becoming violent.</p><p>In the summer of 2023, city leaders faced mounting pressure after repeated teen gatherings downtown led to fights, assaults and other disorder around the Inner Harbor, while a mass shooting at Baltimore’s annual Brooklyn Day celebration that left two people dead and 28 others wounded intensified concerns about keeping young people safe during the summer.</p><p>City officials brainstormed, and came up with a plan that included relying on violence interruption teams comprising school staffers and volunteers from community groups to patrol downtown, and limiting police interaction with teens. The result?</p><p>“We saw a notable decrease in violence and crime in and around our downtown and inner harbor in the months that we have staff out there,” says Stefanie Mavronis, director of the Baltimore mayor’s office of neighborhood safety and engagement.</p><p>By the end of summer of 2023, youth-involved homicides dropped by 83% compared to the prior summer, according to Baltimore city data.</p><p>As Chicago struggles to find ways to rein in teen gatherings that become chaotic and violent, it can look to places like Baltimore for innovative approaches. Experts say a strategy that broadens summer activity choices and job opportunities can be far more effective than an over-reliance on law enforcement and punitive action.</p><p>At the heart of the challenge that teen takeovers pose is the balance between creating for teens living in crime-ravaged neighborhoods safe spaces to get together, while ensuring so-called “teen trends” that become violent don’t cast a pall on downtown commerce and tourism.</p><p>“Socially disadvantaged kids live in neighborhoods with concentrated poverty. I’ve interviewed them,” says Sara Thomas, a research assistant professor in the Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences at Northwestern University. “They have to stay home to avoid violence. They don’t have opportunities. That gets pretty frustrating.</p><p>“We are seeing a concerning lack of spaces where kids on the South and West Sides can gather,” Thomas adds. “My guess is that some of these kids — if they don’t think they’re going to grow up — [figure], `Why not try this risky thing?’ A bad idea that gets thrown out on TikTok suddenly becomes a good idea.”</p><p>The Sun-Times reached out to officials in several cities coping with teen trends. Here’s a look at those cities’ experiences:</p><h3>In Baltimore, keeping teens ‘safe, keeping them engaged’</h3><p>Baltimore has steered clear of expanded youth curfew in favor of its “two-fold strategy” that pairs a neighborhood safety and engagement office and more late-night activities for teens.</p><p>The city’s 25-week safety strategy over the summer includes violence interrupters who go out on weekends to patrol downtown. The teams are made up of some school staff, volunteers and community organizations “who work with our young people,” Mavronis said. Baltimore has prioritized limiting police interactions with teens.</p><p>“Our number one priority is keeping them safe, keeping them engaged and making sure at the end of the night everyone’s getting home safely,” Mavronis said.</p><p>The strategy, launched in 2023 and expanded last year, has so far worked, according to Mavronis.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div </div><p>Earlier this spring, Baltimore officials learned through social media that a “teen takeover” was planned at the Inner Harbor. Before the advertised start time, outreach workers were already on the ground talking with arriving teens.</p><p>Those interactions are designed to go beyond crowd control. Outreach workers ask young people whether they have a safe way home, whether they need help finding jobs, mental health services or other support at home.</p><p>“Sometimes they’re surprised to see us,” Mavronis said of teens who encounter outreach workers during gatherings. “But we’re also not just engaging them. We’re connecting them with resources.”</p><h3>Detroit’s tack — parental responsibility, safe spaces</h3><p>Detroit uses a carrot-and-stick approach. They’ve added youth programming and ramped up curfew enforcement. The stick also applies to parents. Unlike Chicago, Detroit recently enacted a parental responsibility ordinance that fines parents $250 if their children are out after curfew and being disruptive or violent.</p><p>The “carrot” comes in the form of Mayor Mary Sheffield’s “Occupy the Summer” initiative, which offers free recreation, sports, arts programming and other organized activities aimed at giving teenagers safe places to spend their evenings and weekends. City officials say the goal is to make structured opportunities readily available before young people turn to social media-organized gatherings.</p><p>At the same time, Detroit has paired that investment with a renewed emphasis on curfew enforcement and parental responsibility. Police detain juveniles found violating the city’s curfew and issue citations to parents under the city’s longstanding parental responsibility ordinance if their children are out after curfew and involved in disruptive or violent behavior.</p><p>The curfew change, enacted last summer, now carries a $250 fine, with subsequent violations subject to higher penalties. That’s an increase from the previous $75 first-time fine.</p><h3>DC’s get-tough approach draws blowback</h3><p>Newly appointed U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro, a former judge, prosecutor and Fox News commentator, has increased enforcement of the district’s curfew law to prosecute parents who “facilitate, enable, or knowingly permit” their children to engage in “delinquent acts.”</p><p>Washington D.C. recently expanded the district’s curfew to apply to 17 year olds and weekend nights. It also now allows the district’s police chief to declare extended curfew zones in public areas where young people are gathered.</p><p>District leaders said the changes were prompted by repeated large youth gatherings that disrupted downtown neighborhoods, transit stations and commercial corridors, arguing police needed greater flexibility to intervene before crowds became violent.</p><p>Juvenile justice advocates, including the ACLU of DC, have criticized the tougher approach, arguing that curfews and prosecutions disproportionately affect Black teenagers. The group has argued that curfews do little to address the reasons young people gather and that the city should invest more heavily in youth programs, mental health services and other community-based supports.</p><h3>In Philly, a community center to prevent curfew violations</h3><p>In April 2023, a so-called flash mob in Philadelphia wreaked havoc that resulted in requiring teens under 18 to be accompanied by an adult after 2 p.m. at major shopping malls. Like Chicago, Philadelphia has a curfew of 10 p.m. for kids under 18. But the turn-in time for kids 13 and under is 9:30 p.m.</p><p>A non-profit in Philadelphia also offers an evening community resource center between 6 to 9 p.m. for teens to avoid curfew violations. The center stays open until 2 a.m. for “police curfew handoffs.”</p><p>Philadelphia’s mass transit system, SEPTA, restricts the use of student discounted fare cards to school days between 5:30 a.m. and 8 p.m. In May, they launched a crackdown on student-involved fare evasion that cost the system $11 million a year, which came with a side benefit of making it more difficult for teens to congregate in large downtown groups.</p><h3>Chicago’s experience with teen takeovers</h3><p>Chicago’s struggles with large gatherings of teens began in the 1990s along North Michigan Avenue. Then-Police Superintendent Garry McCarthy moved quickly to safeguard the Magnificent Mile, Chicago’s marquee shopping district, from groups he called “flash mobs.”</p><p></p><p>The hard-nosed approach got political support from then-Mayor Rahm Emanuel — and it worked.</p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p> The pandemic denied teens access to the social interactions that young people crave. Today, they have fewer public places to gather safely without getting in trouble. Media coverage of disruptive teen gatherings that intimidate older adults has prompted more restrictions at the public places where young people love to gather.</p><p> </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-c10000" name="image-c10000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/fabb4ce/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0a%2F9e%2F04e3c8304140be829380a71b9f75%2Fteentakeover-260526-17.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/447d974/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0a%2F9e%2F04e3c8304140be829380a71b9f75%2Fteentakeover-260526-17.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f09f94f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3000x1684+0+158/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F0a%2F9e%2F04e3c8304140be829380a71b9f75%2Fteentakeover-260526-17.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Hundreds of young people gather near the Griffin Museum of Science and Industry in the Hyde Park neighborhood as Chicago police officers attempt to disperse them, Monday, May 25, 2026. On the Near West Side, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/24/cpd-officers-hurt-near-west-side-gathering" >a car veered </a>into five Chicago police officers and injured them as they tried to disperse an unruly crowd of youths. Those arrests did not prevent an even bigger crowd from <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/25/large-crowd-causes-lake-shore-drive-closure-at-57th-street" >overtaking the 57th Street Beach</a> in Hyde Park and spilling onto Lake Shore Drive. </p><p>Afterward, Mayor Brandon Johnson argued again that throwing the book at young people and their parents is not the answer class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson, shown here with then Chicago police Supt. Larry Snelling, has resisted calls for expanded curfews to deal with teen takeovers. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Former Philadelphia Police Chief Charles Ramsey believes the “permissiveness” of politicians like Johnson is at least part of the reason why the problems of destructive and potentially violent teen trends appear to be getting worse.</p><p>“People are afraid to do anything. They want to complain about it. But they don’t want to do anything. That includes some elected officials,” Ramsey says. “They’re afraid they’re going to piss off the base. We get too hung up on that stuff. We want to give everybody a break and be too soft on everything, and we’re losing it as a society.”</p><p> Ramsey said he is not saying “send people to Alcatraz.” But he was adamant that “there needs to be some consequences” for kids and parents who look the other way — “even if it’s probation where a kid is not able to go out after a certain hour or associate with other kids known to be involved” in causing trouble.</p><p>“The parent needs to take some action against their own child. Don’t let them go on the internet for a period of time. Take away the cell phone,” adds Ramsey, who once worked as a Chicago deputy police superintendent. “ </p><p>Thomas says she believes the pandemic and school closings it triggered had a profound effect on young people whose still-developing brains she likened to a “car with a sensitive gas pedal and faulty brakes.” That means they’re “inclined to take big risks when there are apparent social rewards” like approval of friends, even if those friends are “endorsing a bad idea.”</p><p>Young people are hungry for safe alternatives in their own neighborhoods so they don’t have to go downtown to meet people, Thomas says. They need jobs that give them skills, a sense of accomplishment and a chance to earn money, she said.</p><p></p><p>Media coverage of teen gatherings has made adults wary whenever they see large groups of young people in a public place. But Thomas warns, “The more we treat kids as scary, the scarier they’re going to get. These are human beings. These are kids. I’ve spoken to them about gun violence and their motivations to carry guns. Every one of them didn’t want to carry guns. They only carry them because they’re scared.”</p><h3>Chicago takes a cue from Baltimore</h3><p>Vaughn Bryant, vice president and executive director of Metropolitan Peace Initiatives, said his community violence intervention network has formed a crisis prevention unit that includes a 20-member team on call to assist the Chicago Police Department.</p><p>Their biggest concern is teens and young adults who “come to trends to settle disputes and instigate conflicts,” some of them gang-related. All it takes is “two-to-four people in conflict” for things to “go awry,” Bryant said.</p><p>“CPD started calling us to send CVI workers to large downtown gatherings. That’s why we formed a team to do that. It’s unique to Chicago to have a non-police response — a community response to teen trends,” said Bryant, whose network of organizations has $9 million in annual contracts with the city.</p><p>“Often there are multiple trends on the same weekend. We go to ones that are potentially larger and at risk of violence. We engage with youth [that] we get to know and de-escalate any conflicts we see. We figure out where they’re from and what their interests are. entries.title: Oak Lawn man’s death tied to mid-July heat wave: ‘He had a good amount of life left in him’
entries.summary: <p>Joseph W. Huff was just getting settled into his retirement years when he died inside his Oak Lawn home earlier this month.</p><p>His first pension check arrived the same week Oak Lawn police officers found him dead while conducting a wellness check, according to his son and local police. An autopsy determined Huff, 65, died from heat stress and cardiovascular disease. He’s the eighth person in Cook County to die from heat-related causes so far this month, according to the Cook County medical examiner’s office.</p><p>“I just feel like it was too soon, he had just turned 65,” said his son, Joseph Huff. “In my eyes, he had a good amount of life left in him.”</p><p>He last spoke to the elder Huff on Father’s Day in mid-June, which they now believe could have been just days before he died.</p><p>The elder Huff was found inside his Oak Lawn home on July 14, the day temperatures reached 96 degrees at nearby Midway International Airport, according to the National Weather Service and the Cook County medical examiner’s office.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-c00000" name="html-embed-module-c00000"></a><div style="min-height:851px" id="datawrapper-vis-sD1Di"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/sD1Di/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-sD1Di"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/sD1Di/full.png" alt="Heat-related causes have killed eight people in Cook County so far this year, all in July (Locator map)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>His death occurred as the Chicago area was experiencing a heat wave with the maximum temperature at O’Hare International Airport falling just a few degrees shy of the record <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/14/near-record-breaking-heat-expected-as-sizzling-heat-wave-continues" target="_blank" ><u>100 degrees</u></a>, set in 1998. The area also experienced an air quality alert that week.</p><p>The extreme heat in July has been tied to the highest number of deaths in a single year in more than a decade, according to a WBEZ and Sun-Times analysis of data from the Cook County medical examiner’s office. In 2019 and again in 2022, six people died from heat-related causes .</p><p>The others whose deaths in July have been attributed to the heat are: Stephanie Rodriguez, 45; David Gonzalez, 44; Barbara Whigham, 71; Mike Rodriguez, 57; Daniel Machnikowski, 69; Victor Ferguson, 48; and David P. Sopys, 46.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-830000" name="html-embed-module-830000"></a><div style="min-height:527px" id="datawrapper-vis-c2yn0"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/c2yn0/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-c2yn0"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/c2yn0/full.png" alt="Eight people have died from heat-related causes in Cook County so far this year, all in the past few weeks (Column Chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>The younger Huff said his family isn’t sure when exactly his father died, though they believe he could have been dead for as long as weeks before police officers found him. His father didn’t have any pre-existing health conditions they knew of and wasn’t taking medications.</p><p>His dad spent years working in factories where employees learn to work in heated conditions — so if anyone knew how to prepare for the heat, it would have been his dad, the younger Huff said. “The way it happened, how quick it happened … it’s still really shocking.”</p><p>The elder Huff lived inside a trailer that did have air conditioning, but the younger Huff didn’t know if his father’s unit worked well enough to cool the home or if it had stopped working. The trailer was damaged this summer during one of the storms, he said.</p><p>The younger Huff said his father kept to himself but would go out of his way to help someone else.</p><p>“He just had a big heart,” he said.</p><p>While he’s still trying to make sense of his father’s death, the younger Huff said he hopes it spurs people to check on their neighbors, especially the elderly.</p><p>“We need to come together as a society and try to make things better on our own,” he said.<br></p>

entries.title: Bears boss George McCaskey umpired for Savannah Bananas at Wrigley Field
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> chairman George McCaskey got quite the warmup for training camp — he spent three days at Wrigley Field umpiring games played by the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/arts-and-culture/2026/07/25/savannah-bananas-wrigley-field-chicago" target="_blank" >Savannah Bananas</a>.</p><p>McCaskey, who is an umpire and referee for youth and high school sports, was asked to umpire the baseline for three sold-out games against the Firefighters. The Bananas play a high-energy style of baseball that, among other things, rewards outs made by trick plays and counts balls caught by fans as outs.</p><p>Cubs legends Kerry Wood, David Ross and Ben Zobrist made appearances on the field, too — the same way the Bananas brought out former White Sox players to play last year at Rate Field. McCaskey was featured briefly on the Bananas' broadcast.</p><p>Split, the Bananas mascot, posed for a photo with McCaskey and said the chairman replaced his yellow football with a Bears one.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Bears owner George McCaskey didn’t like my green and yellow football… so we threw that one away and he gifted me this one. <br><br>…and yes he’s an umpire in today’s game. <a href="https://x.com/hashtag/dabears?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">#dabears</a> <a href="https://t.co/8dYxIsm6AY">pic.twitter.com/8dYxIsm6AY</a></p>— Split (@kingofpotassium) <a href="https://x.com/kingofpotassium/status/2081124352481792270?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">July 25, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>McCaskey told the Bears web site this week that he marveled at the yellow-clad crowd while on the field.</p><p>"Everybody's happy, everybody's smiling, everybody's having a good time,” he said. “And I thought, 'How lucky am I? I'm not cool enough for this.'"</p>
